body: After a little more research into it, it may be a box bug and unrelated to rclone. I assume that would mean that timestamps in a crypt remote are not encrypted/obfuscated since the issue happens in a box crypt remote as well.

Yes I think this is a problem with box...  I had a look through their docs and I could find anything related.

Below is the result of the failing transaction with `-vv --dump bodies`.

Note what rclone sent `1944-01-01T01:01:00+01:00`

And the response from box `"Invalid value '-820540740'. Value must be greater than or equal to 0"` which implies that box converted that time into a `time_t` and then rejected it because it was before the epoch 1970-01-01.

I tried sending the file to drive and it was OK.  There maybe other remotes which do have a problem - I didn't do an exhaustive survey yet...

What do you think rclone should do here?  I could put a flag in `--local-truncate-old-times` say, which would make the local disk read timestamps before 1970 as 1970-01-01. The rest of rclone would have to treat that date specially and ignore it so it isn't completely trivial...

Or maybe I could get the box backend to put dates before 1970 as 1970-01-01 and make that date be ignored in the syncing routines so files with that date will get synced as size only...

I posted [a message on the box developer forum](https://community.box.com/t5/Box-Developer-Forum/API-I-don-t-seem-to-be-able-to-store-dates-before-1970/m-p/56035#M4613) to see if anyone can throw any light on the matter.

body:
Let me see if I understand exactly what you mean with `--local-truncate-old-times`. You would use it with `rclone copy` or `rclone sync` for example, and it would upload files with the 1970-01-01 timestamp without changing the files on the local disk, correct? Then during `rclone sync`, for example, it would have to recognize that despite differing timestamps between local and remote, there is no synchronization to be done. Or would it fool rclone into thinking the local timestamps were 1970-01-01?

Considering my experience with Box so far, as well as not having seen any issues brought up about this with Box before now, I don't expect this to ever get fixed on their end. So having a workaround with rclone could be a good feature. More-so if there are other cloud providers with the same bug.

For the time being, I just saved the metadata with timestamps into a text file and then `touch`ed all the files from before 1970 so that I could finish my sync. If the data cannot be uploaded with old times, I figure there is little point in keeping the old timestamps on my local files and having a local and remote that differ even when "in sync". I can restore the old timestamps in the event that Box fixes the bug.

I found this on the [Box API reference page](https://developer.box.com/reference#date-format):

> Box supports the subset of dates after the start of the Unix epoch: 1970-01-01T00:00:00+00:00 (00:00:00 UTC on January 1, 1970).

So, I guess we could consider timestamps before 1970 officially unsupported by Box.

> Let me see if I understand exactly what you mean with --local-truncate-old-times. You would use it with rclone copy or rclone sync for example, and it would upload files with the 1970-01-01 timestamp without changing the files on the local disk, correct? Then during rclone sync, for example, it would have to recognize that despite differing timestamps between local and remote, there is no synchronization to be done. Or would it fool rclone into thinking the local timestamps were 1970-01-01?

Having thought about it a bit more, I think I would do this
  * when the box backend reads a date pre-1970 convert it into 1970-01-01 00:00:00 - the "epoch"
  * teach the core sync routines to ignore an "epoch" date
    * this would mean that if the source or the destination had an epoch date on a file the sync routines would not use the date.  Effectively this would mean this would be a --size-only sync for this file.

This then doesn't require a flag.

It doesn't change the timestamps of your local files but they will be set to the epoch at box.

It would mean that if you ever changed the timestamp of these files to > 1970 the timestamp wouldn't get updated.

It might be better to use a date which isn't exactly the epoch as the magic "ignore" date, say 1970-01-01 01:01:01 as dates with the epoch aren't uncommon to see when C programs go wrong!

Eg on my hard disk the epoch and 1 second past the epoch seem like popular times...  No idea where those 1966 times came from!

```
$ find /home/ -mtime +14600 | TZ=UTC xargs -d"\n" ls -l --full-time
-rw-rw-r-- 1 ncw ncw 1406 1970-01-01 00:00:00.000000000 +0000 /home/...
-rw-r--r-- 1 ncw ncw  473 1970-01-01 00:00:01.000000000 +0000 /home/...
-rw-r--r-- 1 ncw ncw  364 1970-01-01 00:00:01.000000000 +0000 /home/...
-rw-rw-r-- 1 ncw ncw  380 1966-10-03 13:54:48.000000000 +0000 /home/...
-rw-rw-r-- 1 ncw ncw  380 1966-10-05 09:03:32.000000000 +0000 /home/...
-r--r--r-- 1 ncw ncw  222 1970-01-01 00:00:00.000000000 +0000 /home/...
```

This appears to be a problem with Opendrive as well, although the effects are somewhat different.  Attempts to use `rsync sync` with files having a timestamp that is before the unix epoch results in the file being retried over and over, uselessly wasting bandwidth and delaying progress of the sync.

And then it tries and fails 10 more times to completely re-upload the file again before finally moving on.

> And then it tries and fails 10 more times to completely re-upload the file again before finally moving on.

Ouch! The opendrive backend shouldn't be retrying 400 errors. That would be easy to fix if you want to send a PR.

https://github.com/rclone/rclone/blob/57c10babfe219be9679e1fe75e3f4338f0a9732c/backend/opendrive/opendrive.go#L649

I'm guessing the comment was originally copied from the amazon cloud drive backend.

That leaves the existing issue of how to deal with out of range timestamps...

Of the ideas above this is the one I like the best

> Or maybe I could get the box backend to put dates before 1970 as 1970-01-01 and make that date be ignored in the syncing routines so files with that date will get synced as size only...

However I think the box and opendrive backends should return these times to rclone as the go epoch `0001-01-01 00:00:00 +0000 UTC` which will mean that [time.IsZero](https://golang.org/pkg/time/#Time.IsZero) will be true.

Then getting the sync routines to ignore dates which satisfy `t.IsZero()` seems sensible.

So

- get box and opendrive backends to
    - if given a time before 1970 write that to cloud storage as 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC
    - if reading a file from cloud storage as 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC then return a Go Zero time

- get syncing routines to
    - if modTime.IsZero() ignore it
 
https://github.com/rclone/rclone/blob/57c10babfe219be9679e1fe75e3f4338f0a9732c/fs/operations/operations.go#L187

Want to have a go at this @eharris ?

issue.body:
This type of error is unlikely to be an error that can be resolved by a retry, and is triggered in #2296 by files with a timestamp before the unix epoch.  This does not address the underlying timestamp issue that #2296 describes, only avoids that issue triggering useless retries.

#### What is the purpose of this change?

OpenDrive previously retried 400 errors, but that should probably not be the case, and at least in the case of #2296 it is quite detrimental.

#### Was the change discussed in an issue or in the forum before?

body: Actually, I just tested opendrive, and it seems that any upload of a file with a mtime less than 100 seconds (from unix epoch) fails with a 400 error code.  This value of 100 seems to be arbitrary and completely undocumented as far as I can tell.

@ncw Can you please also add the "Remote: Opendrive" tag to this ticket?

I received a response from opendrive support regarding the limitation of only being able to store timestamps 100 seconds after unix epoch.  Here was their response:

> This is a limitation of a legacy version of our API. It does seem possible to remove this limitation now. We have added this as a feature request to be included in a release in the next couple of months.

Since they are taking it as a feature request, I also suggested they add the ability to support fractional seconds, to at least microsecond resolution.
